sections.html:
Texas has no state property tax. What you owe is the sum of separate levies from the county, your school district, usually a city, and sometimes a hospital, junior college or other special district, all applied to the same house.

Value comes from the local appraisal district, whose chief appraiser looks at every parcel as it stood on January 1 and also processes exemption requests. A review board settles disputes. In many places the county tax assessor-collector sends a single combined statement each October on behalf of all the units.

Ten dates cover most of what a homeowner needs to remember.

Texas property tax dates for a homeowner
DateWhat happens
Jan. 1Value, exemption status and the year's tax lien are fixed
Apr. 1 or soon afterValue notices go out for single-family homesteads
Apr. 30Deadline for many exemption applications
May 1 or soon afterValue notices for other property
May 15Protest deadline, unless 30 days after the notice is later
July 25Chief appraiser certifies the roll
Sept. 29Most units adopt rates by this date, or within 60 days of the roll if later
Oct. 1Bills mailed
Nov. 30 and June 30Halves of a split payment
Jan. 31Final day without delinquency

The bill shows up in October and is due when you get it. You have until the end of January before penalties begin.

Before voting on a rate, most units calculate two benchmarks once they receive the certified roll. This process is called truth-in-taxation.

One benchmark is the no-new-revenue rate, which would bring in the same dollars from the same properties as last year. The other is the voter-approval rate, a ceiling that voters must clear if a unit wants to exceed it. Most non-school units may grow operating revenue 3.5 percent over the prior year under that ceiling, with extra room for debt service. Junior college districts, hospital districts and certain other special units are allowed 8 percent. A unit that goes over must put the question to voters on the next uniform election date.

  • Both benchmark rates are posted on each unit's homepage.
  • Every notice gives the date of the vote.
  • All but very small units hold a public hearing.

A rendition is a listing of business and other personal property, and it matters far less to a homeowner than to a business. The filing period opens January 2 and closes April 15 for most property types, though the chief appraiser must stretch that to May 15 if you ask in writing. A landlord with equipment or an owner with business furnishings may need to file. An ordinary homeowner generally does not.

If anything is still owed when January ends, the account is delinquent the following day. Six percent penalty and one percent interest are added at once. After that the penalty rises by one percent each month until it hits twelve percent in July, while interest continues monthly with no cap.

When the unit has hired a collection lawyer, up to a fifth more can be tacked on. Because a bill must give you 21 days, one mailed after January 10 delays the delinquency date. A bill dated January 15, for example, goes delinquent March 1.

Homeowners who are older or disabled can split the bill in four, with the first piece due by February 1 and the others on March 31, May 31 and July 31. A late installment costs six percent plus one percent monthly interest.

  • Penalty and interest can be waived if you pay within 21 days of learning about the delinquency and ask in writing before day 181.
  • Some collectors offer payment plans of up to 36 months, and a residence homestead is entitled to one.
  • The four-part option for a current bill is open to owners past 65 or disabled.

The homestead exemption takes the biggest bite out of taxable value. Each school district shields $140,000 of it, and any other unit can add a local cut of up to 20 percent, with a floor of $5,000.

  • Owners 65 or older, or with a qualifying disability, get another $60,000 off the school bill.
  • A service-connected disability rating earns $5,000 to $12,000 off, and a homestead owned by someone rated 100 percent is fully exempt.
  • A surviving spouse who is at least 55 can sometimes keep the late spouse's over-65 benefit.

Applications are generally due by the end of April. If you buy a house after January 1 and the seller never applied, you can still claim the exemption for that year.

sections.h2: What happens if taxes are never paid
sections.html:
Expect delinquent notices first, then perhaps a payment plan, then a lawsuit with court costs piled onto the balance. The suit can end with an auction conducted by a constable or a contracted agent. Sales are announced locally, so watch the county clerk and tax office websites.

Rights after the sale depend on what kind of property it was. Homestead, agricultural and mineral land can be redeemed within two years, and the former owner also has two years to claim excess sale proceeds. If you inherit a house with unpaid years on it, call the tax office quickly, because a payment plan may still be available.

sections.h2: Limits on how fast a homestead bill can grow
sections.html:
There are two protections. After a homestead exemption has been in place a year, the appraised value can rise no more than 10 percent annually, apart from new improvements.

People past 65 or disabled also get a school tax ceiling frozen at the year they qualified, and part of that ceiling can follow them to a new Texas home. Counties, cities and junior college districts may set up their own ceilings, so ask each one if it has.

sections.h2: If the appraisal looks too high
sections.html:
Take it to the appraisal review board, normally by May 15 or one month after the notice if that is later. If the board's decision still leaves you unhappy, you can go to district court, request regular binding arbitration, or, when the board's value is above $1,000,000, use the State Office of Administrative Hearings.

Before any appeal, pay at least the undisputed part of the tax so the account does not go delinquent. Our separate protest guide walks through the hearing itself.

sections.h2: Selling a house with taxes owed
sections.html:
Since the lien rides with the property, no title company will insure a sale until old years are paid. The owner on January 1 stays liable for that year's tax even after a sale and can be sued for it.

Closing usually works like this: the title company pays any delinquent amount from the seller's proceeds and divides the current year between buyer and seller. Request a tax certificate from the assessor-collector that lists every unit, then compare it with the settlement statement.

  • Check for delinquent years, penalties and attorney fees.
  • Ask if the account is on a payment plan.
  • The buyer applies for the homestead exemption after closing.

An owner with back taxes who does not want to deal with repairs, showings or a lender's timeline can consider a cash sale. The balance comes out of the proceeds at closing either way.

faqs.q: Does Texas collect a state property tax?
faqs.a: No. The state levies none. Local taxing units set rates and collect the money.

faqs.q: When is Texas property tax due?
faqs.a: Bills go out in October and are payable on receipt. Anything unpaid after January 31 becomes delinquent on February 1. Where split payment is offered, the halves fall on November 30 and June 30.

faqs.q: How much is the late charge?
faqs.a: On the first day of delinquency a six percent penalty and one percent interest apply. The penalty then grows one percent monthly until it reaches twelve percent in July.

faqs.q: How big is the homestead exemption?
faqs.a: School districts exempt $140,000, plus $60,000 more for owners who are older or disabled. Other taxing units may add local exemptions.

faqs.q: Can back taxes come out of a sale?
faqs.a: Yes. The title company normally pays them from the seller's proceeds, because the lien stays with the house.
